roots.name: My own habit or rule is the universal standard
roots.explanation: Students apply whole-number rules, personal viewpoints, or convenient choices as if they were universal, so they miss that units, position and conventions matter.

roots.name: Things must look like what they are
roots.explanation: Students judge category, function or measurement by visual shape or appearance, so they miss that properties depend on what a thing does rather than how it looks.

roots.name: Numbers and signs ignore units and meaning
roots.explanation: Students treat quantities, rates and signed numbers as plain numbers, mixing up totals with rates and ignoring units, direction or cancellation.

roots.name: Science words mean what they mean daily
roots.explanation: Students read technical terms like speed, heat or circular motion through everyday usage, so they miss the precise scientific definitions.

roots.name: Bigger or more always means stronger effect
roots.explanation: Students assume increasing size, thickness, amount or distance always increases the outcome, overlooking other factors and the actual relationship involved.

roots.name: What I see shows the whole story
roots.explanation: Students treat what is visible or most obvious as complete, so they assume one property applies or that unseen things do not exist.

roots.name: Properties are substances that get used up
roots.explanation: Students treat electricity, energy or magnetism as a physical stuff stored in objects that is consumed or depleted, rather than as a process or property.

roots.name: Effects need direct contact or colliding sources
roots.explanation: Students picture forces, currents and fields as physical things that touch, meet or travel, and they place the importance at one central spot.

roots.name: Natural means safe, good and unchanging
roots.explanation: Students treat natural things as harmless, superior or rigid, and assume extreme conditions never change how things behave.

roots.name: One powerful person controls everything directly
roots.explanation: Students believe a single leader or controller causes every action and rule, which hides distributed roles, social systems and indirect processes.

roots.name: One example speaks for the whole group
roots.explanation: Students generalize from one member, themselves or a prominent case to an entire category, ignoring variation among members.

roots.name: Simple majority voting defines fair rule
roots.explanation: Students equate democracy and participation with one-person-one-vote or majority will, overlooking representation, rights and other forms of participation.

roots.name: Protection works by blocking or absorbing danger
roots.explanation: Students imagine safety devices stop hazards by physically blocking, storing or attracting them, rather than by redirecting or breaking the cause.

roots.name: Having or collecting means owning
roots.explanation: Students merge ownership, possession, wealth, power and revenue rights, so they cannot separate different kinds of authority over resources.

roots.name: If I can't see it, it doesn't matter
roots.explanation: Students assume small, hidden or minor parts and effects are absent or unimportant, and only the most prominent factor counts.

roots.name: Problems only happen in extreme, specific cases
roots.explanation: Students think phenomena, dangers and help are limited to dramatic situations or particular people, missing that they occur commonly and broadly.

roots.name: Everything behaves like a familiar thing
roots.explanation: Students transfer the behavior of fluids, sound or shiny objects to light and waves, assuming one familiar model fits every phenomenon.

roots.name: Strong or willful always wins out
roots.explanation: Students equate strength, power or willpower with outcomes, ignoring that results depend on distinct quantities and underlying processes.

roots.name: The environment is a fixed, uniform background
roots.explanation: Students see surroundings as static, passive and uniform, so they ignore slow change, selective effects and how things interact with their setting.

roots.name: New or human-made always works better, faster
roots.explanation: Students assume technology can copy nature quickly, replaces the old completely, and works like familiar systems, including needing a medium.

roots.name: Relationships are simple, linear and symmetrical
roots.explanation: Students assume interactions need matching properties and that changing one quantity changes another in direct proportion.

roots.name: The past was just like today
roots.explanation: Students project modern institutions, roles, timescales and thinking onto earlier times, so they misjudge how different and distant the past was.

roots.name: Appearances reveal how industry and work operate
roots.explanation: Students infer production, ownership and pollution from what looks obvious, assuming workers, owners and purposes fit simple familiar roles.

roots.name: What seems true or popular is true
roots.explanation: Students accept personal experience, common belief or sweeping statements as proven fact without testing them against evidence.

roots.name: Plants are simple, passive and unlike animals
roots.explanation: Students treat plants as inactive objects or as animals with human-like senses, intentions and processes, missing how living things respond differently.

roots.name: Hot or bright always causes the effect
roots.explanation: Students link heat, light or cold to causes as active substances, so they misattribute effects to hot or fiery sources.

roots.name: Size decides importance and whether it runs out
roots.explanation: Students assume only large things matter and that large resources are endless, while other resources are simply used up.

roots.name: Living things need one outside source
roots.explanation: Students believe nutrition and production come from one specific input taken in from outside, overlooking how organisms make or combine what they need.

roots.name: Visible effort or position means real work
roots.explanation: Students equate looking busy, rank or personal checking with actual productive contribution, confusing effort with its defined result.

roots.name: Past social systems were fixed and hereditary
roots.explanation: Students think historical roles, religions and institutions were rigid, inherited and unchanging, missing flexibility and variety over time.

roots.name: One treatment or cause covers all similar things
roots.explanation: Students lump related illnesses, treatments, and processes together and miss that each needs its own specific cause, remedy, and purpose.

roots.name: Cleaning or renewing means one simple complete process
roots.explanation: Students treat purification, recycling, and refining as a single total removal of dirt, missing that they involve different steps and never give perfect purity.

roots.name: People act for one obvious, practical reason
roots.explanation: Students reduce historical motives, wealth, and rules to a single visible reason like money or power, overlooking religious, cultural, and social purposes.

roots.name: Conflict is always total, simple, and one-sided
roots.explanation: Students assume wars have one motive and end in complete destruction of the loser, missing alliances, negotiation, and varied outcomes.

roots.name: Scarcity and poverty have one simple cause
roots.explanation: Students attribute shortage and deprivation to natural lack or personal failure, ignoring social, economic, and policy causes.

roots.name: People in the past were less capable than us
roots.explanation: Students judge earlier societies as unintelligent, unskilled, or unhygienic, overlooking their deliberate skills and sophisticated achievements.

roots.name: Old things served the purposes modern things do
roots.explanation: Students project present-day functions and assumptions onto ancient structures and objects instead of considering their original context and varied uses.

roots.name: Every official rule or body works the same way
roots.explanation: Students blur distinctions among laws, courts, police, and hierarchy, assuming all legal parts carry punishment, finality, and the same authority.

roots.name: Power flows from one central source
roots.explanation: Students think a single connection or center supplies everything, missing that systems work through complete circuits, multiple parts, and distributed roles.

roots.name: The visible carrier is what causes the effect
roots.explanation: Students confuse the thing carrying something with its source or mechanism, assuming transport means the carrier moves or produces the cargo.

roots.name: All things in a category are the same
roots.explanation: Students overgeneralize from one example, treating all microbes, diseases, environmental problems, or green areas as harmful or identical.

roots.name: Outputs must mirror or equal the inputs
roots.explanation: Students expect a process's result to match or be identical to what goes in, missing that systems transform inputs and results differ across people.

roots.name: The world and records were always as today
roots.explanation: Students assume present conditions and complete written knowledge existed in the past, overlooking change over time and gaps in evidence.

roots.name: Obvious extremes or inaction are the only options
roots.explanation: Students see responses as passive versus violent or effortless, missing active, nuanced approaches and that doing nothing or ignoring something has effects.

roots.name: Natural features follow one simple pattern
roots.explanation: Students assume rivers and water bodies share one origin, direction, name, or nature, ignoring how geography varies.

roots.name: History is made by modern-style, famous, male actors
roots.explanation: Students project present boundaries and identities and focus on prominent men and wars, overlooking women, ordinary people, and complex pasts.

roots.name: The most famous name is the first or cause
roots.explanation: Students credit the best-known person, group, or event with starting everything, ignoring earlier, lesser-known contributors and complex origins.

roots.name: Money terms mean one simple thing
roots.explanation: Students conflate related financial ideas like payment, price, interest, and money, missing their distinct definitions and effects.

roots.name: One visible part does the whole job
roots.explanation: Students assign a whole function to a single organ or simple structure, missing that systems rely on many cooperating parts without conscious intent.

roots.name: What I personally see applies everywhere
roots.explanation: Students generalize from their own limited everyday experience to all places and conditions, missing exceptions and wider contexts.

roots.name: Trade is simple, local, and one-directional
roots.explanation: Students picture exchange as small-scale, one-way, or gift-like, overlooking long-distance, mutual, and structured commercial relationships.

roots.name: Social structures are fixed and uniform
roots.explanation: Students believe social rules, classes, and groups stayed rigid and unified, overlooking change, exceptions, and diversity across time and regions.

roots.name: Governments simply provide and help everyone
roots.explanation: Students assume state actions are free, benevolent, and universal, overlooking costs, motives, and who actually pays or benefits.

roots.name: What is visible or advertised shows reality
roots.explanation: Students take brand names, ads, and visible faces at face value, missing the hidden structure and real operations behind them.

roots.name: One source supplies or creates everything
roots.explanation: Students credit a single central item with producing or providing all of something, ignoring conversion, multiple contributors, and other inputs.

roots.name: Things are wholly good or wholly bad
roots.explanation: Students sort substances, labels, and states into purely good or bad, missing that context, amount, and meaning determine their value.

roots.name: Big results need big, visible causes
roots.explanation: Students expect important things to start large or look dramatic, overlooking small beginnings, scale differences, and gradual effects.

roots.name: Local loss or separation means total ending
roots.explanation: Students equate disappearance, risk, or division in one place with complete destruction or isolation, ignoring degrees and other causes.

roots.name: Names and categories reveal importance or location
roots.explanation: Students infer a thing's rank, location, or type from its label or surface features, rather than from its actual inputs and role.

roots.name: Things that look alike are the same kind
roots.explanation: Students group space objects and missions by appearance or popular depictions, missing differences in type, purpose, and method.

roots.name: Complex processes are simple, uniform, and the same for everyone
roots.explanation: Students flatten multi-part, varying systems (sleep, brain, age) into one simple, constant, single-cause story.

roots.name: Things that seem useless, plain, or harmless have no properties
roots.explanation: Students dismiss byproducts, waste, and familiar substances as valueless or non-chemical, missing their real properties, uses, or risks.

roots.name: Famous, powerful people and titles are always invincible and honorable
roots.explanation: Students take titles, fame, and heroic status at face value, assuming success, pride, and noble motives without checking history.

roots.name: Bad outcomes mean foolishness, accident, or total failure
roots.explanation: Students explain failures by simple labels like madness, luck, or fuel, ignoring reasoned plans, systemic causes, and partial successes.

roots.name: Names and tools are judged by appearance or origin
roots.explanation: Students classify or assign function by surface features, source, or look rather than by actual purpose, process, and content.

roots.name: Each thing does only one job
roots.explanation: Students assign a single function or process to an organism, hormone, or agent, missing that it does several, even opposing, roles.

roots.name: Familiar everyday words mean one simple, obvious thing
roots.explanation: Students apply the everyday meaning of terms like fossil, soil, or underground, missing the broader or more precise scientific meaning.

roots.name: Loss, change, or breaking apart is always harmful
roots.explanation: Students assume losing, dividing, or varying is purely negative, missing the benefits, adaptations, and regeneration involved.

roots.name: Rulers in power acted kindly for the people's benefit
roots.explanation: Students assume colonial authorities had benevolent or single, simple motives, missing exploitation, control, and the many causes of conflict.

roots.name: Official terms have narrow, ideal meanings
roots.explanation: Students read terms like migration, reservation, and reserved forests in a narrow or idealized way, missing their wider scope and actual purpose.

roots.name: Words imply extremes: all or nothing, always or never
roots.explanation: Students turn partial or periodic ideas like seasonal, census, or search for resources into total absence, constant repetition, or one simple meaning.

roots.name: Work without visible ownership or payment has no value
roots.explanation: Students overlook the effort, investment, and function behind informal, unpaid, or intermediary roles because they lack a shop, pay, or property.

roots.name: The most striking, popular example represents the whole category
roots.explanation: Students generalize from the brightest, most famous, or most familiar image, mistaking appearance and popularity for the true nature of things.

roots.name: What suits one special case applies to everyone
roots.explanation: Students over-generalize a specific use, feature, or method as universally true or best, ignoring context and starting conditions.

roots.name: Things happen because of need, storage, or simple possession
roots.explanation: Students attribute change to purpose and value to holding or storing, missing the real mechanisms like chance, acceptance, and transfer.

roots.name: Today's outcome was the original intention all along
roots.explanation: Students read the present result back into the past, missing that goals and plans changed gradually over time.

roots.name: Freedom means no rules or limits at all
roots.explanation: Students equate independence and rights with absolute, unconstrained action, missing that freedoms have limits, accountability, and sometimes opposite aims.

roots.name: Rural people all share one simple, uniform situation
roots.explanation: Students stereotype rural life as only farming, landlessness, or one kind of work, missing the diversity of occupations and schemes.

roots.name: All technology works in one familiar way
roots.explanation: Students assume every medium or device is two-way, purely informative, immaterial, or connected, missing real differences in how they function.

roots.name: A law's scope is narrow and its effect automatic
roots.explanation: Students assume laws cover only one group or setting, work in one direction, or end a practice simply by banning it.

roots.name: Big, visible institutions are simple, singly owned, and benevolent
roots.explanation: Students assume large organizations have one owner, a public purpose, or helpful motives, missing profit goals and complex ownership.

roots.name: Messages that seem personal or friendly are trustworthy
roots.explanation: Students trust contact that feels personal, kind, or comes from friends, without checking source, intent, or who a service is for.

roots.name: Language stays fixed and uniform across time and place
roots.explanation: Students assume one unchanging, elite language was used by everyone, missing how languages evolve and vary with region and audience.

roots.name: Our own or the Western culture invented everything important
roots.explanation: Students credit major inventions to their own culture or to Europe, missing earlier or independent origins elsewhere.

roots.name: Institutions have one simple source of money and loyalty
roots.explanation: Students assume media serve one funder, one form, or one master, missing advertising revenue, many formats, and independence.

roots.name: Objects serve only one fixed purpose
roots.explanation: Students assume tools and materials have a single use and become useless once flawed, missing their varied and adaptable uses.

roots.name: Old, familiar materials were always the same and dominant
roots.explanation: Students assume iron dominated early eras and equate it with steel, missing the timeline of materials and the role of alloys.

roots.name: Objects have a single obvious purpose, like money or beauty
roots.explanation: Students assign small or shiny artifacts one plain function, missing their other roles like administration or status.

roots.name: Historical rulers fit simple, familiar patterns of lineage and origin
roots.explanation: Students assume rulers were related in neat succession and were native, missing unclear lineages and foreign dynasties.

roots.name: Royal objects and lands belong personally to the king
roots.explanation: Students treat symbols and land grants as personal possessions or furniture, missing their state, symbolic, or administrative roles.

roots.name: Art and writing from the past served only religion
roots.explanation: Students assume historical creators worked only on sacred themes, missing the social, political and everyday subjects they also addressed.

roots.name: Anyone who opposes a tyrant must be democratic
roots.explanation: Students treat political labels as simple opposites, overlooking that rulers' enemies and allies can be internal, and that overthrowing one power does not make another democratic.

roots.name: Newer methods or corrections only replace or subtract
roots.explanation: Students think updates remove things or make old methods obsolete, rather than adding to or extending what already exists.

roots.name: The outermost or biggest-looking thing is the greatest
roots.explanation: Students confuse position, frequency or appearance with magnitude, mixing up location, count and size.

roots.name: Opposite sides are always perfectly symmetrical
roots.explanation: Students assume opposing sides or reflections match exactly, ignoring real differences in geography or the way mirrors actually reverse left and right.

roots.name: Official projects are always good and fair for everyone
roots.explanation: Students assume authority-backed development brings only benefits and fair treatment, overlooking costs borne by people and environment.

roots.name: Social bias terms only mean negative, hateful things
roots.explanation: Students equate stereotype and prejudice with insults or hatred, missing that prejudgments can also be positive.

roots.name: Similar-sounding bodies or wrongdoings are all the same
roots.explanation: Students lump together different organisations or kinds of cheating instead of distinguishing their separate roles and meanings.

roots.name: Services and legal help always cost money
roots.explanation: Students assume every service or court requires heavy fees and professionals, ignoring free or low-cost options.

roots.name: Mathematical terms must match their everyday tidy meanings
roots.explanation: Students let the everyday sense of a word like curve override its precise definition, excluding shapes that are valid.

roots.name: A copy or record is just like the original
roots.explanation: Students assume representations, such as shadows or printed slips, match the original in form or purpose, ignoring how they differ.

roots.name: A substance is only in the obvious foods
roots.explanation: Students believe a substance is present only in its best-known or tasty source, overlooking hidden sources like tea, cola or savoury foods.

roots.name: Early or simple-looking art was made casually by children
roots.explanation: Students equate simple or ancient styles with childish play, underrating the skill and purpose of early human work.

roots.name: One famous leader is responsible for everything in an era
roots.explanation: Students credit all achievements and texts of a period to its best-known ruler, ignoring other people and contexts.

roots.name: Destructive processes can only cause harm
roots.explanation: Students see things like fire as purely destructive, missing their role in renewal and managed use.

roots.name: Extreme environments are empty and uniform
roots.explanation: Students picture harsh places like deserts as barren and the same everywhere, ignoring their variety and life.

roots.name: Different named categories are the same thing
roots.explanation: Students merge distinct categories, such as seasons, because they are related or overlap in topic.

roots.name: A word for a body means the building it meets in
roots.explanation: Students mistake an institution's name for a physical office, confusing the group of people and its function with a place.

roots.name: Old situations never change; the past still applies
roots.explanation: Students hold on to outdated facts about a country's dependence, missing how circumstances have changed over time.

roots.name: Composite measures are just one simple measure
roots.explanation: Students reduce an index with several components to a single familiar factor like income.

roots.name: Institutions only hold things and never use them
roots.explanation: Students think banks simply store deposits and don't realise money is lent out and circulated.

roots.name: Group schemes run on outside help, not members' own contributions
roots.explanation: Students think community schemes are charity from outside, missing that members' own savings fund them.

roots.name: Each task needs its own separate procedure
roots.explanation: Students assume every situation has its own number or step, missing that unified systems can handle all of them.

roots.name: Only the best or most visible are checked
roots.explanation: Students think checks focus on top performers, when scrutiny often covers others and is random or broader.

roots.name: A country's projects are built only by that country
roots.explanation: Students assume national missions use only homegrown parts, ignoring international collaboration.

roots.name: Machines keep working forever
roots.explanation: Students assume devices last for years, ignoring the limited lifetimes imposed by harsh conditions and power.

roots.name: People will act well without any preparation
roots.explanation: Students think good responses to crises happen naturally, without planning or coordination.

roots.name: A system is one single unit
roots.explanation: Students see a system as a single block, missing that it consists of separate cooperating parts.

roots.name: Unit conversions are simple powers of ten
roots.explanation: Students guess conversion factors by assuming round numbers, without checking the actual relationship between units.

roots.name: A bond is a physical connection between two things
roots.explanation: Students imagine bonds as tangible links limited to two items, rather than attractive forces acting more widely.
